ARM has been around as a platform since '85, was revolutionary, but ultimately could not compete with the steam building behind x86. But with x86 getting all the consumer base, they had to make sure the evolution of their architecture remained backwards-compatible with the 8086 and IBM's original design ideas. To this day x86 chips boot up in a mode that can only address 64K of RAM at a time, and several rounds weird opcodes actually gets it into "Long" mode where it's actually a 64-bit chip.

ARM didn't have the focus that x86 had until PDAs started to take off. That started putting a truly "personal" computer in to people's hands. Then they bolted on cellular radios and you got smartphones. Then Android and iOS dropped on their respective hardware, and holy fuck did a whole lot more people get on board. Now ARM has that consumer base to get stupid amounts of R&D money. And better yet, they have no legacy bullshit to worry about like x86. Fresh, clean designs, no baggage.

Not all ARM implementations are equal (especially as ARM goes mixed-core, something x86 can't do!), and Apple's choice to fab their own has resulted in the most power ARM cores on the planet, capable of challenging some x86 chips. Apple will never license their tech to others, so a round of clones are going to need to come out (they get quicker every year) before this shit really takes off in a laptop. It's an inevitability at this point, x86 is losing its performance crown with every microcode patch that goes out to make the things secure enough to use, killing yet another bit of its performance edge.
